parakeet: People often assume there's one big moment that makes somebody leave their faith. A debate you watched, a book you read, a tragedy that shakes you to your core. And sure, for some people, it happens just like that. A single event flips the switch. But for me, it was different. My deconversion didn't come through a debate stage or a philosophy book. It came through something far more personal. It came in hospital rooms with my heart racing as doctors fought to bring my children into the world. It came in late night conversations at the edge of a child's bed when curiosity left me with no choice but to answer honestly. It came in the quiet but heavy responsibility of realizing I could either hand my kids the same prepackaged beliefs I grew up with, or I could give them the freedom to think for themselves. The secret catalyst to my deconversion wasn't doubt alone. It wasn't even disappointment in religion. It was fatherhood. Becoming a parent forced me to confront every crack in my theology. Every birth, every question, every promise to be honest with my children pulled me further away from faith and deeper into truth. All four of my children came into this world through C-sections. That wasn't what I imagined when I thought about fatherhood. In my mind, childbirth was supposed to be this natural, beautiful process, maybe even a sacred one. But from the very beginning, it was anything but predictable or smooth. Each birth was surrounded by danger. Each time I was reminded that life is fragile, that survival is never guaranteed.
